stories.title: Marcus & Millichap Arranges Sale of Multifamily Portfolio in Illinois
stories.excerpt: Marcus & Millichap announced the sale of a 134-unit multifamily portfolio in Berwyn and Maywood, Illinois. “This transaction highlights the continued demand for multifamily assets in western Cook County, where investors remain attracted to strong suburban fundamentals and convenient access to Chicago,” said Sam Antreasian, director of investments. “By acquiring 134 units across five buildings in a single transaction, the buyer gains immediate scale with opportunities to unlock additional value through the portfolio’s diverse unit mix and upside potential.”Antreasian, Ryan D. Engle and Andrean Angelov, investment specialists in Marcus & Millichap’s Chicago Oak Brook office, procured the buyer, a private local investor with ambitious growth plans in the immediate market. The portfolio consists of five apartment buildings totaling 134 units across Berwyn and Maywood. The portfolio unit mix consists of 36 studios, 77 one-bedrooms, 20 two-bedrooms, and one office suite. If you’re reading about the multifamily industry, you should be in the room with its leaders. Connect Apartments brings together the executives featured in Connect CRE’s coverage for an afternoon of high-level insights and unmatched networking on September 22 at The Biltmore in LA. The post Marcus & Millichap Arranges Sale of Multifamily Portfolio in Illinois appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Marcus & Millichap sold 134-unit portfolio across five buildings in Berwyn and Maywood, Illinois
Western Cook County suburbs remain attractive to investors seeking scale and portfolio upside
Multi-property consolidation enables buyer to capture value through unit mix and operational leverage
stories.summary: Marcus & Millichap arranged the sale of a 134-unit multifamily portfolio in western Cook County, Illinois (Berwyn and Maywood), highlighting sustained investor appetite for suburban Chicago assets. The buyer acquired five buildings in a single transaction, gaining immediate scale and optionality to unlock value through diverse unit mixes and upside potential. The deal signals continued fundamentals strength and convenient access to downtown Chicago remain competitive advantages for suburban Cook County.
stories.impact: Portfolio consolidation at scale in western Cook County indicates strong institutional capital competition for stabilized suburban supply. Developers should monitor appetite for value-add opportunities and ground-up development feasibility in high-demand Cook County submarkets where institutional buyers are actively deploying capital and targeting portfolio economics.

stories.title: Silicon Valley Light Industrial Refinanced for $10M
stories.excerpt: Gantry secured a $9.65-million permanent loan to refinance maturing debt from the acquisition of a two-building, infill light industrial property located at 2290 De La Cruz Blvd in Santa Clara. Principal Tony Kaufmann and associate Jake Davis with Gantry’s San Francisco production office represented the borrower, a private real estate investor. The 10-year, fixed rate, non-recourse loan was secured from one of Gantry’s correspondent insurance company lenders with 30-year amortization. Gantry will service the loan for the lender. The property is 100%-leased in a long-term agreement to a national auto collision repair business. The property totals 37,600 square feet across two buildings, including a recently constructed 11,500-square-foot building addition. Kaufmann said, “This is one of those unique properties in Silicon Valley, where similar building inventory available to non-tech or AI-related tenants is at a premium due to voracious tech user demand. After reviewing various options for the site, including redevelopment for tech-related uses, an experienced sponsor saw the advantage of land banking the asset by expanding and renovating the existing light industrial buildings for non-tech uses.” The post Silicon Valley Light Industrial Refinanced for $10M appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Gantry secured $9.65M permanent refinance for Santa Clara light industrial property, 37,600 SF
Tech user demand in Silicon Valley is pricing out non-tech tenants; sponsor chose industrial expansion over tech conversion
Long-term lease to national auto collision repair business, 30-year amortization, 10-year fixed-rate financing
stories.summary: Gantry closed a $9.65 million permanent refinance for a two-building, 37,600-square-foot light industrial property in Santa Clara, California, on behalf of a private investor. The property includes a recently constructed 11,500-square-foot building addition and is 100% leased long-term to a national auto collision repair business. Rather than redeveloping for tech/AI uses, the sponsor opted to land-bank and renovate for non-tech industrial tenants, recognizing scarcity value in non-tech building stock amid voracious tech user demand.
stories.impact: Silicon Valley's acute shortage of non-tech-aligned industrial and light manufacturing space creates defensive income-generating opportunity for specialists serving regional repair, logistics, and service businesses. Developers should identify underutilized industrial properties that can be repositioned for non-AI/tech tenants at premium rents and extended lease terms as tech users consolidate premium space.

stories.title: NYC Taxi and Limousine Commission Takes 39K SF at AmTrustRE’s 250 Broadway
stories.excerpt: This TLC wasn’t exactly chasing waterfalls, just a new office. The New York City Taxi and Limousine Commission is relocating to AmTrustRE’s 250 Broadway across the street from City Hall Park in Manhattan’s Financial District, the property owner announced Thursday. The TLC is relocating its headquarters from another FiDi office at 33 Beaver Street and will occupy the entire fourth floor and a portion of the fifth floor of its new building. The space includes a variety of private offices, conference rooms and a hearing room for public proceedings, according to AmTrustRE. The agency is expected to move into 250 Broadway in the first quarter of 2027. The length of the lease and the asking rent were not disclosed. The average asking rent for office space in the Financial District was $60.61 per square foot during the first quarter, according to Colliers data. AmTrustRE was represented in-house by Anne Holker, and by Brad Gerla, Michael Rizzo and Alex Benisatto from CBRE. The tenant was represented by Gus Field from Cushman & Wakefield. The brokers did not immediately respond to requests for comment. “The Financial District remains one of Downtown Manhattan’s most sought-after office markets, and this lease underscores the strong demand we’re continuing to see for high-quality workplace environments in the neighborhood,” Holker said in a statement announcing the lease. “We’re pleased to welcome TLC to 250 Broadway, where they join a dynamic mix of public and private sector tenants. We look forward to supporting their success and building a long-term tenancy.” This deal brings 250 Broadway, a 31-story, 648,000-square-foot office tower, to 90 percent leased. Other tenants in the building include coworking company WeWork, law firm Rose & Rose, and academic publishing company IGI. Amanda Schiavo can be reached at aschiavo@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: NYC Taxi and Limousine Commission leasing 39,000 SF across two floors at 250 Broadway, Manhattan Financial District
TLC relocating from 33 Beaver Street; move-in Q1 2027; lease terms not disclosed
Financial District office asking rent averaged $60.61/SF in Q1; government tenant signals ongoing mixed-use occupancy demand
stories.summary: The NYC Taxi and Limousine Commission is relocating its headquarters to 250 Broadway in Manhattan's Financial District, occupying the entire fourth floor and a partial fifth floor (39,000 SF total). The agency is moving from 33 Beaver Street and will occupy private offices, conference rooms, and a hearing room, with occupancy expected in Q1 2027. Financial District average asking rents were $60.61/SF in Q1; specific lease economics were not disclosed.
stories.impact: Government tenant absorption at flagship Financial District addresses supports mixed-use office reactivation but does not directly signal apartment demand. The lease activity indicates continued public-sector demand for Financial District presence and may support auxiliary service workers and visitor traffic that could have modest downstream benefit to neighborhood multifamily fill and neighborhood vitality.

stories.title: Medford Food Processing Facility Trades Amid Interest from Local and National Investors
stories.excerpt: Marcus & Millichap closed the sale of 93 Mystic Ave., an industrial property dedicated to food processing use in Medford, MA. The sale price was $5 million. “This rare, core-located food processing facility drove interest from local, regional and national investment groups,” said Mattias Edenkrans, associate director investments in Marcus & Millichap’s Boston office. “With the sellers targeting a sale process free of development permitting, we identified a group that was able to provide immediate non-refundable deposits and close cash within 45 days of offer acceptance.” Edenkrans and Luigi Lessa of Marcus & Millichap exclusively marketed the property on behalf of the seller, 93 Mystic LLC, and procured the buyer, a private family.   The 19,278-square-foot property sits on a 1.12-acre lot. Built in 1950 and 1955, it comprises two buildings, the main 14,278-square-foot building and a 5,000-square-foot auxiliary building. The property was delivered vacant and is currently designed for food processing with minimal office space. The post Medford Food Processing Facility Trades Amid Interest from Local and National Investors appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Marcus & Millichap sold 93 Mystic Ave., Medford, MA food processing facility for $5 million
19,278 SF property on 1.12 acres comprises two buildings; built 1950–1955; delivered vacant
Buyer was local private family; seller prioritized quick close (45 days) over entitlement/development risk
stories.summary: Marcus & Millichap closed the $5 million sale of a 19,278-square-foot, dual-building food processing facility in Medford, Massachusetts. The property, built in 1950 and 1955 on 1.12 acres, comprises a 14,278-SF main building and a 5,000-SF auxiliary structure. The seller targeted a rapid, non-development-contingent sale process, and the buyer—a local private family—closed within 45 days of offer acceptance, indicating strong local investor appetite for industrial real estate free of regulatory encumbrance.
stories.impact: Limited relevance to multifamily development. The transaction reflects industrial asset demand but does not signal broader commercial real estate financing, cost, or demand shifts affecting apartment supply in greater Boston.

stories.title: WICo Opens Target at Site of Former Perris Movie Theater
stories.excerpt: Wood Investment Companies, Inc. (WICo) announced the opening of a new 149,655‑square‑foot Target at Plaza de Perris, located at 1688 N. Perris Blvd. in Perris. The store opening marks a significant milestone for the center and the surrounding Inland Empire communities, according to WICo.. Target now occupies the former Regency Theatres building, which WICo demolished to make way for the retailer’s new store following the theater’s 2024 closing after nearly 30 years. Plaza de Perris totals nearly 300,000 square feet and is anchored by Burlington, Food 4 Less, Ross, Planet Fitness and Five Below. Patrick Wood, president of WICo, said the opening represents a transformational moment for the community. “Redeveloping the former Regency Theatres into a state‑of‑the‑art Target has been a priority for us and for the City of Perris,” said Wood. “This project reflects years of collaboration, planning and investment, and we’re proud to deliver a flagship retailer that elevates daily shopping options for residents throughout Perris and the greater Inland Empire.” The post WICo Opens Target at Site of Former Perris Movie Theater appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: WICo opened 149,655 SF Target at Plaza de Perris, Perris, California; demolished former Regency Theatres
Plaza de Perris is 300,000 SF; anchored by Burlington, Food 4 Less, Ross, Planet Fitness, Five Below
Retail repositioning reflects Inland Empire demand recovery and consumer traffic consolidation around discount/value retail
stories.summary: Wood Investment Companies (WICo) opened a new 149,655-square-foot Target at Plaza de Perris in Perris, California, occupying the site of the former Regency Theatres, which closed in 2024 after 30 years. The shopping center totals nearly 300,000 square feet and is anchored by Burlington, Food 4 Less, Ross, Planet Fitness, and Five Below. The redevelopment signals the city and developer's collaboration to attract flagship retail and transform the community's daily shopping experience.
stories.impact: Limited direct relevance to multifamily development. Retail anchor stabilization supports neighborhood viability and may modestly increase worker demand (lower-wage retail jobs), but does not signal housing supply pipeline, population in-migration, or rent growth drivers specific to Inland Empire apartment markets.

stories.title: Entre Commercial Realty Completes Sale of IOS Facility in Spring Grove
stories.excerpt: Entre Commercial Realty recently completed the sale of a 20,500-square-foot outside storage facility at 2500 Westward Drive in Spring Grove, Illinois. Sam Deihs and John M. Joyce of Entre Commercial Realty represented the seller, and Adam Fortino of Keller Williams Commercial represented the purchaser. The property features two buildings with eight drive-in doors and a fenced yard on 1.92 acres, making it a desirable asset for industrial users seeking outside storage service capability. Entre was able to capitalize on the strong demand for IOS assets, securing multiple offers and selling the property to a local material-handling company in need of outdoor storage. stories.title: Delshah Capital Acquires Five Upper West Side Apartment Buildings for $37M
stories.excerpt: Michael Shah’s DelShah Capital is back at it again with another multi-address, multifamily acquisition. The real estate private equity and asset management firm paid Quality Capital USA $36.9 million for five residential buildings just west of Central Park on Manhattan’s Upper West Side, according to property records filed Thursday. The first batch of six-story apartment buildings are at 3-5 West 108th Street and 7-9 West 108th Street. The two neighboring buildings span a total of roughly 48 market-rate and rent-controlled units, according to New York City Department of Finance records. The second collection resides eight blocks south and contains a total of approximately 99 units at 4 Manhattan Avenue, 8 Manhattan Avenue and 10-16 Manhattan Avenue. Delshah’s purchase is a more than $20 million discount on the portfolio’s last sale in 2018, when Quality Capital USA paid Orbach Group $57 million across five transactions. Orbach had acquired the buildings between 2013 and 2015 for a collective $36.15 million. Delshah has embarked on somewhat of a shopping spree this year. Just this month, Delshah purchased three mixed-use residential properties in Brooklyn’s Williamsburg neighborhood for $128 million. Three months earlier, the firm acquired a 142-unit multifamily property in the same neighborhood for $76 million. In February, Delshah offloaded the $364.7 million Park Hill Apartments complex on Staten Island, a move that coincided with CO’s report that the firm was poised to enter the Class A office market through an in-contract, $135.7 million deal with A.M. Property Holding Corporation for the 24-floor office component of Tishman Speyer and GIC’s CitySpire tower. Spokespeople for Delshah and Quality Capital did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Delshah Capital acquired five Upper West Side apartment buildings for $36.9 million; ~147 units total across two locations
Portfolio includes 48 units at 3–9 West 108th Street and ~99 units at 4/8/10–16 Manhattan Avenue; mix of market-rate and rent-controlled
Purchase reflects $20M+ discount versus 2018 sale price ($57M); represents institutional value-add repositioning in Manhattan core
stories.summary: DelShah Capital paid Quality Capital USA $36.9 million for five residential buildings on the Upper West Side just west of Central Park in Manhattan. The portfolio spans two clusters: roughly 48 units at 3–9 West 108th Street and approximately 99 units across 4, 8, and 10–16 Manhattan Avenue. The 2024 acquisition represents a $20+ million discount from the portfolio's 2018 sale price ($57M to Quality Capital), signaling institutional opportunity in rent-regulated Manhattan assets.
stories.impact: Delshah's acquisition at a substantial discount to prior sale price signals distressed owner motivation and investor willingness to underwrite lower returns in stabilized Manhattan rent-regulated buildings. While this is a value-add play on existing supply, it reflects softer financing conditions and potential cap-rate expansion—conditions that could dampen new development feasibility in Manhattan and shift capital toward repositioning legacy stock over ground-up development.

stories.title: KKR Posts Record Earnings as Fundraising Hits $133B
stories.excerpt: Even as the private equity industry grapples with elevated interest rates and a growing backlog of unsold portfolio companies amid mounting concerns over artificial intelligence’s impact on the software sector, KKR reported record earnings during the second quarter of 2026. Fee-related earnings rose 37 percent annually to $1.21 billion, thanks in part to management fees being up more than 25 percent, while total operating earnings jumped by 29 percent compared to last year to $1.53 billion — the highest quarterly total in the firm’s 50-year history. Revenue jumped to $5.73 billion, up from $5.09 billion a year prior. Quarterly net income increased nearly 40 percent annually to $660.1 million. “Our industry is increasingly K-shaped,” Co-CEO Scott Nuttall said during the company’s earnings call Thursday. “Most of the external focus is going to be on the unhappy part of the K. We find ourselves on the happy part of the K.” KKR sold stakes in eight companies, including Japanese semiconductor manufacturing company Kokusai Electric and Korean shipbuilder HD Hyundai Marine Solution. Although KKR’s opportunistic real estate portfolio posted a 1 percent gross loss in the second quarter, it generated a 1 percent gross return over the past 12 months. KKR raised $34 billion in new capital during the quarter, bringing its 12-month fundraising total through June to a record $133 billion. The investor is making inroads in AI infrastructure, having committed and invested over $75 billion across digital infrastructure and power to date. In the coming decade, company executives said they envision the infrastructure build-out costing trillions of dollars. In June, it launched a $10 billion company to provide the infrastructure needs for the build-out of data centers. bullets: KKR reports record Q2 2026 earnings: $1.53B operating earnings, $1.21B fee-related earnings (up 37% YoY)
Total AUM fundraising hit $133B; revenue jumped to $5.73B from $5.09B YoY despite elevated rates and AI uncertainty
Co-CEO Nuttall notes K-shaped market: 'most external focus on unhappy part; we find ourselves on happy part'
stories.summary: KKR posted record second-quarter 2026 earnings with total operating earnings of $1.53 billion (up 29% YoY) and fee-related earnings of $1.21 billion (up 37% YoY). Management fees rose more than 25 percent annually, and the firm raised $133 billion in new capital. Despite industry headwinds—elevated interest rates, a growing backlog of unsold portfolio companies, and AI concerns—KKR co-CEO Scott Nuttall characterized the firm as positioned on the 'happy part of the K' in a bifurcated market.
stories.impact: Mega-cap PE fundraising strength and record earnings signal robust capital availability for large-scale multifamily platforms and value-add plays despite rate environment. Developers should monitor KKR and peer PE appetite for apartment platforms, development partnerships, and repositioning opportunities—elevated dry powder and management fee pressure may accelerate deployment in stabilized and value-add residential assets, competing with traditional debt and equity sources for attractive deals.

stories.title: Karim Alibhai Started at Best Western. Now He Rents Rooms at $2,500 a Night.
stories.excerpt: As room rates at the world’s poshest properties push past $2,000 a night, Karim Alibhai has been snapping up high-profile luxury hotels. Alibhai has built an $8 billion portfolio that includes properties from Chicago to Bermuda to Costa Rica. His company, Gencom, this year paid $320 million for the Ritz-Carlton New York, Central Park. Since 2024, Miami-based Gencom also has acquired the Thompson Central Park and the InterContinental New York Times Square, along with the Ritz-Carlton Key Biscayne in South Florida. Not bad for someone whose first job in the hospitality industry was managing a Best Western. A native of Kenya, Alibhai attended Rice University in Houston and now lives in Coral Gables, Fla. Commercial Observer caught up with the CEO this week to ask about Gencom’s $1 billion in acquisitions in New York City the past two years, as well as rising room rates, the K-shaped economy and the evolution of his career. The following conversation has been edited for length and clarity. The Ritz Carlton Key Biscayne. Commercial Observer: You’ve taken on $1 billion in acquisitions in the past couple of years. What’s driving your deals? Karim Alibha: I think it’s a combination of a few things. One is market driven. So, for example, in New York City, that’s a market we identified with one of the lowest supplies in 25 years, and demand was looking to increase. So that was a big reason that we went over the past two years and acquired almost $1 billion of hotels in New York City. That was a driver for us. Separately is the leisure resort segment. Since the pandemic, that segment has had the best recovery and has far surpassed other luxury segments. That’s another big driver for us. So it’s really market driven/opportunity driven. I get the sense that the luxury hotel market is resistant to price increases. What are you seeing on the pricing front in terms of room rates? bullets: Karim Alibhai's Gencom built $8B hospitality portfolio; paid $320M for Ritz-Carlton NYC Central Park in 2024
Since 2024, acquired Thompson Central Park, InterContinental Times Square, Ritz-Carlton Key Biscayne; $1B invested in NYC past 2 years

stories.summary: Gencom, led by CEO Karim Alibhai, has assembled an $8 billion hospitality portfolio and deployed $1 billion in New York City acquisitions over the past two years, including the Ritz-Carlton Central Park ($320M in 2024), Thompson Central Park, InterContinental Times Square, and Ritz-Carlton Key Biscayne. Luxury hotel room rates globally have surpassed $2,000 per night, and Alibhai's acquisition pace reflects consolidation of prime hospitality assets in major gateway markets.
stories.impact: Limited direct relevance to multifamily development. Luxury hospitality capital consolidation and rate inflation do not signal apartment demand or supply drivers. However, proximity of trophy hotel assets to multifamily in NYC (Central Park South corridor) may indicate competitive capital allocation between hospitality and residential—developers should monitor whether premium gateway multifamily acquisition appetite softens as alternative asset classes attract mega-cap PE deployment.

stories.title: Declining Empire State Building Visits Drive Q2 Loss for ESRT
stories.excerpt: New York City’s declines in international tourism over the past year since President Donald Trump assumed office are starting to affect Empire State Realty Trust (ESRT)’s finances. The real estate investment trust (REIT) reported second-quarter funds from operations (FFO) of $57 million, or 21 cents per share, marking a loss of $25.8 million or 15 cents per share from the same period a year ago. ESRT attributed the loss largely to a “massive” non-cash impairment charge of $166.11 million connected to underperforming visitations in the Empire State Building observatory stemming from persistent drops in international tourists to the Big Apple. The observatory generated $12.4 million of net income in the first quarter, a sharp 48.5 percent decrease from $24.1 million in the same period in 2025. Visitors to the observatory during the quarter were 450,000, down 28.5 percent year-over-year. In addition to the decline of international visitors to the U.S., ESRT also attributed the profit loss to lower usage of third-party pass program channels used for tourist sites around New York. Such passes are often used by budget-conscious international travelers. “While all attractions have experienced reduced visitorship in 2026, our drop compared to the market in general is larger due to our prior dominance with pass programs and their international presence,” Anthony Malkin, CEO of ESRT, said during the firm’s earnings call early Thursday afternoon. “Softer visitation persisted through the second quarter.” Projections for reduced visits to the observatory prompted ESRT to reduce its 2026 core FFO assumptions to a range of 75 cents to 79 cents per share compared to 85 cents to 89 cents per share FFO in February. bullets: Empire State Realty Trust reported Q2 loss: $25.8M ($0.15/share) vs. $57M FFO gain prior year
Empire State Building observatory visits fell 28.5% YoY to 450K; non-cash impairment charge of $166M on observatory visitation decline

stories.summary: Empire State Realty Trust (ESRT) reported a $25.8 million Q2 loss ($0.15/share) after a $57 million FFO gain in Q2 2025, driven primarily by a $166.11 million non-cash impairment charge on the Empire State Building observatory. Observatory visitation fell 28.5% year-over-year to 450,000 visitors, and net income from the observatory plummeted 48.5% to $12.4 million from $24.1 million, reflecting sharp drops in international tourists to New York City since the Trump administration assumed office.
stories.impact: ESRT's tower losses signal potential secondary effect on Manhattan multifamily demand: declining international tourism reduces visitor-driven spending, ancillary service jobs, and hotel/hospitality employment, which historically support transient and short-term rental demand. Prolonged international tourist weakness could dampen Manhattan apartment rental growth in neighborhoods dependent on visitor-adjacent services and may signal softer net migration into NYC, indirectly affecting multifamily leasing velocity and rent growth in gateway Manhattan markets.
